ON COMPUNCTION: BOOK ONE

1. Blessed Demetrius, when I see you constantly pressing me and demanding, with great urgency, the discourses on compunction, I always count you blessed and admire the purity of your soul. For no one can come to desire such discourses unless he has first been thoroughly cleansed and has risen above all the things of this life. This is easy to see in those who are held by this longing even for a short time. They are changed so greatly and so suddenly that they are carried up to heaven at once. They release the soul from the cares of the world as if from heavy chains, and so let it fly to the place that is its own and akin to it. But for most people this happens only rarely in the whole of their lives, while you [?] of the purity in your soul. [?] the care for others [?]

I welcome [you] for your great [?]. But if you are truly looking to your own good and think you need someone to rouse you, I do not know how you could have shown me more plainly that you need nothing from me. Even so, I will give way and do as you ask, for all these reasons: your boldness before God, your eagerness in asking, and your friendship toward me. In return, repay me with your prayers. Pray that my life may be set right from now on, and that for the present I may be able to say something worthy, something able to raise up souls that lie prostrate and to brace and strengthen those that have grown slack.

Where, then, where should I begin this discourse? What foundation, what groundwork shall I lay for it? Clearly the words of Christ. In them he calls those who laugh wretched and counts those who mourn among the blessed, saying: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted," and, "Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep." And quite rightly. The whole present age is truly a time for mourning, for mourning and lament. Such a calamity has seized the whole world, and such evils hold all people in their grip, that anyone who wished to examine them closely, if a close examination were even possible, would never stop lamenting and mourning. Everything has been so overturned and thrown into confusion, and there is no trace of virtue anywhere.

What is worse, we have no sense of the evils that grip us ourselves, nor do we give others any sense of them. We are like a body that blooms on the outside but is being consumed within by a great fire. In our numbness we are no different from the deranged. They say and do many dangerous and shameful things without fear, yet feel no shame at any of it; they even take pride in it and think themselves healthier than those in their right minds. We are the same: we do everything the sick do, and yet we do not even know that we are sick. When it comes to the body, if some ordinary ailment troubles us, we call doctors, spend money, show endurance, and do not give up, but try everything until we are rid of what pains us. Yet the soul is stung every day, torn apart by the passions of the body, burned, thrown over cliffs, and destroying itself in every way, and we pay it not the slightest attention.

The reason is that the disease has seized everyone. Think of people who are sick in body: if it happened that no healthy person was with them, nothing would stop them all from falling into utter ruin, since no one would be restraining their irrational desires. So it is with us. No one is truly sound in the faith; all are ailing, some to a greater and some to a lesser degree, and so there is no one able to help those who are lying down. If someone came to us from outside, and properly understood the commandments of Christ and the disorder of our way of life, I doubt whether he would think anyone more hostile to Christ than we are. It is as if we had set out to go against his commands, so thoroughly have we traveled that road

So that no one may think my words exaggerated, I will now try to give the proof, and I will take it from nowhere else but from the commandments of Christ themselves. What, then, does Christ say? "It was said to those of old, 'You shall not murder.' But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment, and whoever says to his brother, 'Raca,'" [?]

For we are unwilling to give ourselves the security that comes from obedience, or to do what we have been commanded, and so free our minds from fear of what is to come. Weighed down and choked by conscience, and eager to throw off the great fear of the punishments that await us, we throw ourselves into another pit: we refuse to believe in those punishments at all. People gripped by a high fever leap into cold water, and they do not shake off the burning heat but bring another fire on themselves. In the same way we, stung by the knowledge of our sins, are driven to plunge into a flood of excess, so that from then on we may sin without fear. We are angry with our brothers not only when they are present; often we fight with them even when they are absent, which is the height of savagery. When people greater and more powerful than ourselves wrong and insult us, we bear it with great forbearance because we fear them. But toward our equals and inferiors, who have done us no harm, we are hostile. So much stronger is the fear of men than the fear of Christ.

3. Is there any hope of salvation for us, then, when we show such negligence and contempt? How could there be, tell me? And yet what burdensome or heavy thing has Christ asked of us? "Do not be angry with your brother without cause," he says. That is much easier than putting up with someone else who is angry without cause. In that case the fuel for the fire has already been gathered, but in this case nothing has been laid beneath it, and you light the flame yourself. Enduring without catching fire when someone else brings a torch is not the same as staying quiet and calm when no one is provoking you. Whoever masters the first has given proof of the highest philosophy, while whoever achieves the second deserves no admiration at all. So when we accomplish the greater thing out of fear of men, yet will not do even the lesser one out of fear of God, consider how great a punishment and penalty we make ourselves liable to.

Do not think that "brother" means only your equal or a free man; it means your servant as well. For "in Christ Jesus there is neither slave nor free," as the Apostle says. So even if we rage at our slaves without cause, we will suffer the same penalty. He too is a brother, he has been granted the true freedom, and he has the one Spirit. Who, then, can show a life clean of abuse and of irrational and pointless anger? Do not tell me of someone who gives way to it only rarely; tell me of someone who has never been caught by it at all. Until you show me that, you cannot escape the threat by saying that you do not give way to it constantly. Even if a thief or a fornicator commits that sin only once, he is not let off punishment because he did not dare it often. He is punished because he dared it at all.

And what about the commandment that comes next? What unbeliever would not think it a fable, seeing how violently we overturn it? God said: "If you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift." Yet we come to the altars while at war with one another and harboring hidden hostility. And while God [shows] such [concern for] our reconcil[iation] [?]

4. As for the commandments against swearing, I am ashamed even to mention them, not only because of the oath-taking but also because of the constant perjury. If swearing is a fault and a breach of a commandment even when one swears truly, where shall we place perjury? If whatever goes beyond "yes" and "no" comes from the Evil One, then whose work is what goes even further than that?

Then again he says: "If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well. If anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak too. If anyone forces you to go one mile, go two with him. Give to the one who asks of you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you." What could anyone say to this? At each of these sayings, all that is left is to weep and hide our faces, so squarely have we set ourselves against them. We spend all our time in lawsuits, quarrels, trials and disputes. We cannot bear even a small injury, whether in deeds or in words, but turn savage at the slightest thing.

You may be able to name some who have spent a great deal on the poor and were afterward despised for the poverty this brought them, and suffered countless ills. They will be few, and easily counted. Even so, you have not shown me the philosopher described here, for he lives a far more spiritual life than that. Giving willingly is not the same as bearing being stripped of everything. But why do I say "bearing"? What Christ said goes far beyond even that. His word removes the souls of the wronged so far from anger against those who wrong them that he bids us not only to accept calmly what has already been taken, but also to give up willingly what is left. He bids us to show more eagerness to suffer evil than they show madness in doing it. For suppose a man who wants to do wrong finds his victim more ready to suffer than he wanted. Having had his fill, he sees the injured man generously offering more besides. Then he goes away defeated, blushing at such extraordinary forbearance. Even if he is a wild beast, or something worse, he will be more moderate from then on, because this comparison has shown him clearly his own wickedness and the other man's virtue.

This is the life I am now looking for. I see it set down in the Scriptures alone, nowhere else, and nowhere in practice. Do not tell me of someone who was wronged and put up with it, for that can also happen out of weakness. Someone may even have done this toward his equals, and toward those he could have taken revenge on. But he did not go so far as to outdo the other's desire and give more than was wanted, showing by what he added willingly how patiently he bore what had been taken by force. Higher still, touching the very summit, is this: Christ commanded us to count those who do such things to us, who injure us in our money, our bodies and everything else, among our friends, and our true friends at that. "Do not only give still more to the one who robs and cheats you," he says, "but love him too, with a love" [?]

[?] of these he commanded. If you do him no wrong but turn away from him, and do not look on him kindly, and keep a fresh wound in your soul, you have not yet kept the commandment Christ gave you. How, then, can you beg God to be merciful to you, when you have not yet been merciful yourself to those who have sinned against you? A certain wise man mocks this very thing when he says: "A man nurses anger against another man, and seeks healing from the Lord? He has no mercy on a man like himself, and does he pray about his own sins? Though he is flesh, he keeps up his wrath; who will make atonement for his sins?"

I wanted to fall silent at this point and stop the discourse with what has been said, so ashamed am I, so much do I blush to go further. For the further the discourse goes, the more clearly it shows the war we have taken up against the commandments of Christ, and our enmity without truce. But what is gained by my silence, when the facts cry out about this war so loudly, and when, before the facts themselves, the one who is to judge us knows everything clearly?

As for not storing up treasure on earth but in heaven, one might find some, though few, who have achieved it well. All the rest act as if they had heard the opposite and been ordered to store up treasure on earth: they let go of heaven, cling to everything on earth, chase madly after money, and hate God while they love mammon. As for "Do not worry about tomorrow," I know no one who has either listened to it or obeyed it, because of our little faith. So I will pass over this commandment with my face covered. Christ ought to be believed even when he simply makes a statement. As it is, even when he gives unanswerable reasons and offers examples, the birds and the grass, we do not believe him. Like the Gentiles, perhaps even more pettily, we are gnawed by worry over these things. We were told not even to pray for them, and yet we spend all our energy on them. This commandment, then, as I said, I will pass over with a blush, and go on to those that follow, in case I can find some small consolation for this shame.

What does he say next? "Do not judge, so that you may not be judged." I thought I would find consolation for our shame, but I see an addition to it no smaller than what came before. Even if we had committed no other sin, this alone would be enough to lead us into the depths of Gehenna. We sit as harsh judges of other people's sins while we overlook the beams in our own eyes, and our whole life is spent prying into other people's affairs and condemning them. You would not easily find anyone, whether layman, monk or cleric, free of this sin. And yet so great a threat hangs over it: "For with the judgment you judge, you will be judged," he says, and, "With the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you." This sin brings so great a punishment and no pleasure at all, and yet we all rush toward the evil, as if we were striving and competing to enter the furnace of Gehenna not by one road only but by many. [?]

[?] they did terrible things. We disregard this most fearful commandment not only in dealing with others but also in dealing with ourselves, whenever we must partake of the immortal mysteries. We often do so in the midst of the impurity and shamelessness that weigh upon us.

Nor are these the only commandments one can see overturned by everyone entirely; so are those that follow. Christ said, "Whatever you want people to do to you, do the same to them," and we do everything we do not want done to us. We were commanded to enter through the narrow gate, and everywhere we look for the wide one. That some laypeople embrace and love it is not very surprising. But that men who are thought to be crucified should seek it out more eagerly than they do is truly astonishing; the thing is more like a riddle. Almost all monks, if you ever invite them to take on some ministry, will say this first thing: they ask whether rest is to be found there, and whether the one inviting them can give them rest. The word "rest" is constantly on their lips. What are you saying, man? You were commanded to walk the hard road, and you ask about rest? You were ordered to enter through the narrow gate, and you look for a wide one? What could be worse than such perversity?

But so that you will not think I am saying this to condemn others, I will tell you my own story. Not long ago, when I had decided to leave the city and go to the monks' tents, I was very busy inquiring and finding out where my necessities would come from. Could I eat fresh bread every day? Would anyone make me use the same oil for my lamp and my food? Would anyone push me into the hardship of a diet of pulses, and put me to hard labor, ordering me to dig, carry wood or carry water, and do all the other tasks of that kind? In short, I talked a great deal about rest.

Yet those who take service under officials or the administration of public affairs ask about none of these things. They ask only whether the post brings profit, and profit soon. If they can ever be confident of that, they give no thought to anything else: toil, danger, dishonor, the duties of a slave, long journeys, life in a foreign land, insults, torture, changes of fortune, being disappointed of their hopes at the very end, as often happens, untimely death, separation from their families, being bereft of wife and children, or any other hardship. Frenzied by the desire for money, they endure everything that they expect will get it for them. But we have neither money nor land set before us. We have heaven, and the good things in heaven, "which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the human heart," and yet we ask about rest. So much more pitiable and soft we are than they! What are you saying, man? You are about to be sent to heaven and to receive the kingdom there, and you ask whether there is anything difficult along this road and journey? Are you not ashamed? Do you not blush? Nor, going away [?] you must [?] of those immortal mysteries.

…of Christ. [?] And he said: “In all these things,” he says, “we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.” And do not be surprised. For if friendship between human beings has often made people dare to face death, what would the love of Christ not accomplish? What hardship would it not make easy? So everything was bearable to him, because he looked only to the one he longed for. He held that suffering everything for his sake was greater than any pleasure or enjoyment, as indeed it is. He did not think of himself as being on earth, or in the present life, or living among human beings. It was as though he already held his lot in heaven, lived as a citizen among the angels, had received the kingdom and enjoyed the vision face to face. So he despised both the pleasures and the pains of the present, and he took no account of rest, which we constantly seek. Instead he cried out: “To this very hour we hunger and thirst, we go naked, we are beaten, we are homeless, and we toil, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we appeal.” And again: “We have become like the refuse of the world, the scum of all things, to this day.” Once he had turned the eyes of his soul to heaven and been struck with amazement at the beauty there, he could not bear to turn back to the earth again. Think of a poor and needy man who has been shut up all his life in a dark, lowly hovel. Once he has seen a king gleaming with heaps of gold and flashing gems, he would no longer choose even to call to mind the house of his poverty, but would do everything he could to move to that dwelling, if it were allowed. In the same way that blessed man, having beheld the things in heaven, despised the poverty here. Though the needs of the body made him live among people, he turned toward nothing here, but moved his whole self over to that city. And why do I speak of the pains of the present life? The longing for Christ drew him so strongly that if he had been offered even those undying punishments to endure for Christ's sake, he would never have refused. For he did not serve Christ as we hirelings do, fearing hell and wanting the kingdom. He was seized by another longing, far better and blessed, and he suffered and did everything for no other reason than to satisfy the love he had for Christ. That love mastered his mind so completely that he would willingly be cut off even from what was most precious of all to him, I mean being with Christ, for whose sake he despised both hell and the kingdom of heaven. For Christ's sake he would choose even that unspeakable fall, embracing it as one of the things most to be desired and choosing it with great eagerness. 8. Perhaps what I have said now seems obscure to many. But when I put it more clearly, then it will seem incredible to the very people who found it obscure before. And no wonder. That blessed man too expected to be disbelieved about these things, and so he said in advance: “I am speaking the truth in Christ, I am not lying…” [?] “was, [?] therefore he also said” [?] in Colb. Shortly after, the same: “friendships… made; what would that of Christ not accomplish?” [?] “kingdom [?] and enjoying face to face, thus.” Colb.: “we endure; when defamed, we appeal. Like…” Shortly after, the same: “having turned toward the.” Colb.: “for so strongly did [it] breathe.” Colb.: “mind, by as much as of all.” Below, Morel.: “again willingly to be estranged, choosing for Christ also an unspeakable fall”; [?]: “again to be estranged, to choose with great eagerness, and such a fall for Christ, as one…”

…saying: “That was Paul, that was Peter, that was John.” What does it mean, “That was Paul, that was Peter”? Tell me, did they not share the same nature too? Were they not brought into life by the same way as we were? Were they not raised on the same food? Did they not breathe the same air? Did they not use the same things? Did some of them not have wives and children, others worldly trades, while still others even fell into the very pit of wickedness? “But,” someone says, “they enjoyed a great deal of God's grace.” Well, if we were commanded to raise the dead, or open the eyes of the blind, or cleanse lepers, or make the lame stand upright, or cast out demons, or heal other diseases of that kind, this excuse would have its place. But if what is now at stake is an examination of our way of life and a display of obedience, what bearing could these things have on that? For you too enjoyed divine grace when you were baptized, and you received the Spirit. If not for working signs, then you received enough of it to take up an upright and exacting way of life. So the corruption is due to nothing but our own laziness. On that day Christ does not hand out the prizes simply to those who have worked signs, but to those who have done his commandments. For he says: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” He does not say “because you worked wonders,” but “because I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you took me in; naked, and you clothed me; I was sick and you visited me; I was in prison and you came to me.” And in the Beatitudes too he nowhere puts those who work miracles, but those who lead a life…

9. So even if that grace has now been withdrawn, this cannot harm us at all. But neither can it serve as our defense when we give account for what we have done. For we do not admire those blessed men because of their signs, since that was wholly the work of God's power. We admire them because they displayed an angelic way of life, and that is the work of help from above together with their own effort. It is not I who say this now, but that imitator of Christ himself. When he was writing to the disciples and contending against the false apostles, he wanted to show the difference between genuine and counterfeit ministry. He did so not from the signs but from what he had achieved, speaking thus: “Are they ministers of Christ? I speak as a madman: I am more. In labors far more, in prisons far more, in beatings beyond measure, often near death. Five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I have spent in the deep. On frequent journeys, in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers; in toil and hardship, through many sleepless nights, in hunger and thirst, often in fasting, in cold and nakedness. And apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me, my anxiety for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” This is why I admire the… [?] Colb.: “we were commanded, and the eyes of the blind, and the lame,” etc. Soon after, Colb.: “to those things.” [?]: “was of the grace of God.” [?] “of all the churches”; Morel.: “all the churches.” Shortly after, Colb.: “I; for of these…” [?] Christ says, many [?] the same: “we did; and then I will declare to them, I never knew you; depart.”

…of others, seizing [?] they would let even their own things go at that time. Even if someone chose to set fire to their possessions along with the whole house, they are not stirred. I myself know many who did this after losing those dearest to them. Some exchanged the city and its comforts for life in the country; others built houses beside the tombs of the departed and ended their lives there. But that comes later. While grief is at its height, they care for nothing around them. The madness they once had for managing and amassing money, for gaining power and the glory the crowd bestows, they burn up in the flame of despondency like grass, or the flower of grass, and cast it out of the soul. The mind then passes into such philosophy that it cannot bear even the mention of any of the pleasures of this present life. Everything that seemed pleasant before now becomes repugnant to them and seems utterly bitter. None of the servants or friends would dare then to say a word about the affairs of this world, however urgent. Everything gets out of the way and gives place to talk of philosophy. Through grief the soul is taught then, as though in some sacred place, the nothingness of human nature, the brevity of this present age, the perishable and unstable state of worldly things, the play-acting of the stage on which events unfold. Then there is great contempt for money, then anger is done away with, then ambition is disregarded. Envy cannot lurk inside one crushed by grief, nor can pride drive him into frenzy, nor does desire inflame the licentious. With all these banished from there, a single thought settles in, the one that constantly holds on to the image of the dead. This is food and drink, sleep and pleasure, rest and great consolation; this is glory and wealth, power and luxury. 10. This is how we ought to mourn the loss of our salvation, to say no more. With such longing and eagerness the eye of our soul ought to be fixed entirely there, and everything for us ought to be the remembrance and picturing of it. But as it is, those who have lost children and wives occupy their minds with nothing but imagining the ones torn from them, while we, who have lost the kingdom of heaven, think of anything rather than that. And none of them, even if he happens to be of the most royal family, is ashamed of the law of mourning. He sits down on the ground, laments bitterly, changes his clothing, and submits with great readiness to all the other hardships of that penalty. He takes no account of his upbringing or his bodily condition, or of the illnesses that come afterward from that distress, but bears everything with great ease. And not only men but women too, even very frail ones, show these things and more. But we, mourning not children or wives but the ruin of a soul, and not someone else's soul but our own, make excuses and plead the [?] of the body… “Of the things around them” is absent in Colb. “Become” is absent in Colb. [?] Colb.: “of the great stage.” [?] “more royal.” [?] Colb.: “great, everything.” Savile and Morel.: “great, then he will bear.”

TO STELECHIUS, AND ON COMPUNCTION: SECOND DISCOURSE. 1. Stelechius, holy man of God, how can what you have commanded be done? How can discourses on compunction be brought forth from a soul so weak and cold? I think that anyone who is going to say something noble on this subject must, before everything else, be on fire with this zeal himself and boiling with it, so that his words on these things fall on the souls of his hearers more fiercely than any red-hot iron. But we do not have this fire; everything within is ash and dust. Where, then, tell me, where shall we kindle this flame? We have no spark, no fuel at hand, and no wind coming to fan it, because of the thick mist that the multitude of sins has spread over our soul. I do not know. It would be up to you, then, as the one giving the command, to say how the command might be carried out and reach its proper end; we will supply the service of the tongue. As for you, call on the one who heals the brokenhearted, who gives patience to the fainthearted, who raises the poor from the earth, to kindle in us that fire. It is accustomed to consume all human weakness and to cut away all sleep, listlessness and fleshly heaviness. It lifts the wing of the soul toward heaven, and from that vault, as from some lofty peak, it shows the whole illusion and play-acting of this present life. Whoever has not been able to fly up there, or to sit at this lookout, cannot see the earth or the things on it as they deserve to be seen. Many things darken our sight, many disturb our hearing and trip up our tongue. So one must withdraw from all the turmoil and smoke and retire to that solitude where the calm is deep, the sky bright and clear, and there is no uproar. There the eyes are fixed unwavering, gazing intently at the longing for God, and the ears stand undisturbed, occupied with one thing only: hearing the divine oracles and listening to the all-harmonious spiritual symphony. Its sway so masters a soul once it has been captured that whoever is drawn by that melody takes no pleasure in food or drink or sleep. So neither the uproar of worldly affairs nor the crowding of many bodily concerns could slacken that tension. The clamor rising from the storm below does not reach that height of the soul. Just as those who have moved to the highest mountains would no longer hear or see anything that is done or said in the city… Title in Colb. thus: “Of the same, to Stelechius on compunction.” In Savile: “Of John Chrysostom to Stelechius, and on compunction [?] this.” The same: [?] “and to boil.” [?] “shame, which” [?]. Shortly after, “then” after “it would be” is absent in [?]. Colb.: “and to us from.” And soon after: “the peak of some theatre.” Shortly after, [?] “tripping up; and one must withdraw oneself from all the turmoil and plague to.” [?] “the fear and longing of God.” [?] Below, in Colb., [?] before “and” [?].

For when he says, “The world has been crucified to me,” he means this insensibility. Or rather, not only this one but another like it too, so that the insensibility just described is double. He did not merely say, “The world has been crucified to me,” and fall silent. By what he added he pointed to a second one as well, saying, “and I to the world.” It is great philosophy to regard the world as dead, but greater than this, and far greater, is to be disposed toward it as though one were dead oneself. What Paul indicated, then, is something like this. He says he stands apart from present things not as the living stand apart from those who have died, but as the dead stand apart from the dead. For even if a living man does not desire the one who has died, he still has feelings about him in other ways: he may still admire the beauty of the one lying there, or pity him and weep. But a dead man has no such relation or disposition at all toward the departed. Wanting to show this, he said, “The world has been crucified to me,” and then added, “and I to the world.” Do you see how far he stood apart from the world? How, while walking on the earth, he had leapt up to the very summit of heaven? Do not talk to me about mountain ridges, or glens and ravines and trackless desert. These alone are not enough to rid the soul of its turmoil. What is needed is that flame which Christ kindled in Paul's soul. That blessed man fed it with this spiritual reflection and raised it so high that, starting from the earth below, it reached heaven itself, and the heaven above this, and the one beyond that again. He himself was caught up as far as the third heaven, but his longing and his love for Christ shot beyond not only three heavens but all the heavens. In body he was small, and in that respect he had nothing more than we do; but in spiritual disposition he far outstripped every person on earth. So no one would be wrong to compare that saint to an image like this. Picture a flame that covers the surface of the whole earth and, lifted on high, passes beyond the vault of heaven on every side. It runs through the air above it, whether that is air or whatever it may be, and fills the space between these two heavens with fire. It does not stop its course even there, but leaps up all at once to the third, and makes everything a single pyre, as broad as the whole earth and as high as the distance from the third heaven to us. Or rather, I do not think I have expressed even the smallest part of his love. Anyone who goes through the work written to Demetrius on this very subject will know for certain that these words are no exaggeration. This is how we must love Christ; this is how we must stand apart from present things. The holy prophets too had souls like this, and that is why they received other eyes. Withdrawing from present things was the work of their own zeal. But that other eyes were then opened in them to contemplate the things to come was the work of God's grace. Such was Elisha. He withdrew from all worldly things, fell in love with the kingdom in heaven, and spat upon everything present, kingdom, power and glory… [?] “saying so much.” Below, the same: “dead; the [?].” Colb.: “but through the.” Savile and Colb.: “and all who are.” Colb.: “the breadth,” and below, “the height.” Colb.: “for the [?] fell in love with the way of life.” Below, “I say” after “glory” is absent in [?].

…brings punishment, but mourning and affliction are praised everywhere. All the same, that blessed man cut through all these obstacles and laid hold of compunction so firmly that he showed as much of it in purple, diadem and royal throne as a man sitting in sackcloth and ashes in the desert. It was as if he were one of the ordinary people and had never seen a kingdom, or the luxury of palaces, even in a dream. In those to whom this good thing genuinely comes, it shows as much strength as fire does among thorns. A person may be strangled by countless evils, bound with many cords of sin, burned by a fierce flame of desire, or surrounded by great turmoil of worldly affairs. Even so, compunction at once drives all those things utterly away, as if with a fierce whip, and sets them far from the soul. Just as fine dust could never stand against the force of a violent wind, so the multitude of desires will not be able to withstand the onrush of compunction when it falls on them. They vanish and scatter faster than any dust or smoke. For if love of bodies so enslaves the soul as to lead it away from everything else and nail it to the tyranny of the beloved alone, what would longing for Christ not do, and the fear of being estranged from him? Both these things so turned the prophet's soul that at one time he said: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God”; and again, “My soul thirsts for you like a waterless land”; and, “My soul has clung close behind you”; and at another time, “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, or discipline me in your wrath.” 4. And let no one tell me that he wrote this psalm mourning his sin. That is not true, and the title written above it does not allow anyone to suspect any such thing. If no one could point to a subject written at its head, anyone who wished could fit this psalm to those events. But the psalm spoken about those events is clearly identified, and this one has a different subject. So let us not, I beg you, let us not confuse divine things, or vote that our own reasonings carry more authority than the teachings spoken by the Spirit. What, then, is the title? “For the eighth,” it says. And what is the eighth, but the great and manifest day of the Lord? It burns like an oven; it makes even the powers above tremble (“for the powers of the heavens will be shaken,” it says); it shows fire running ahead of the King on that day. He called it the eighth to indicate that the state of things will be changed and that the life to come will be renewed. For the present life is nothing but a single week. It begins from the first day and ends at the seventh, then turns round again through the same intervals, going back up to the same beginning and coming down to the end. That is why no one would ever call the Lord's Day the eighth day, but the first, for the cycle of the week does not extend to the number eight. “This” is absent in Colb. Soon after, the same: “strangled” [masculine], and “bound” [neuter plural]. [?] “utterly” [singular]. [?] Colb.: “estrangement from there.” Soon after, in the same: “these” [?]. Colb.: “for neither does it allow.” Colb.: “but if the one spoken [about] those things.” Shortly after, the same: “teachings of the Spirit… let us deem our own reasonings more authoritative.” Colb.: “it says, the powers.” [?] “to the end. One would not call the eighth day the [?]”

…one can see the humility of his soul, both from his thinking himself worthy of so great a punishment and from his not daring to ask God for complete forgiveness. That belongs to those who condemn themselves severely and have convinced themselves that they are more sinful than anyone else. And what is greater still: even the mercy of not being punished severely he asks to receive from God's mercy and love for humankind, as one who has grown exhausted. "Have mercy on me," he says, "for I am weak." What is this? The man who received such a testimony, who did not forget God's judgments ("Your judgments," he says, "I have not forgotten"), who shone brighter than the sun: does he speak such words? Yes. For this is the wonderful thing: though he achieved such great things, he never said or thought anything great about himself, but considered himself the last of all, and asked to be saved by God's love for humankind alone. It is as though he were saying: "I deserve a punishment that cannot be escaped, and to be punished forever. But because I can no longer bear it, I ask to be released from my present evils." He is like servants who have done countless terrible things. They could not say that they had not sinned, but because the pain of the whips is unbearable, they ask to be spared any more blows. But I think he is also hinting here at another weakness. What is this? The weakness that arises in him from despondency and lamentation. For when grief falls on us too violently, its excess tends to gnaw away all the strength of the soul. I think the righteous man suffered this too, because he condemned himself so severely and never held out good hopes to himself, but always the opposite. He makes this clear, at any rate, from what follows. "Have mercy on me," he added, "for I am weak. Heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled, and my soul is greatly troubled." And before that he had said, "Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger." But if a man with so pure a conscience asks that his deeds not be strictly examined, what shall we do? We are caught in so many evils, we fall so far short of his confidence, and we have not shown even the smallest part of his confession. Why, then, did the blessed man confess in this way? He had been taught that no one will be justified before God, and that even the righteous man is scarcely saved. That is why he pleads at one time, "Do not enter into judgment with your servant," and at another, "Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak." 5. This is worth noticing everywhere: he nowhere mentions his own good deeds, but casts his salvation on God's love for humankind. This is the mark of a contrite soul and a humbled spirit. This is what makes one who achieves great things fear and tremble more than sinners do. And to see that he trembled and feared in this way [148], hear him saying: "If you mark iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall stand?" For he knew, he knew clearly, that we owe God many debts, and that even the smallest sins deserve great punishment. Foreseeing from on high, he knew what Christ would lay down as law when he came: that a severe [penalty] is set not only for murders, but also for insults, abuse, evil thoughts, laughter, untimely speech, jesting, and still smaller things [?]. This is clear from what follows: "Have mercy [?] for [?]" [?], having first [?] "rebuke me" [?] the blessed man [?] before God. Therefore he pleads (some words omitted). [?] your servant into [?]; that even the righteous man is scarcely saved; therefore [?] with fear in this way [?]. Below: further, if Christ [?] not of murders [?] and jesting [?]. Each of them from them [?].

…so that, as lord of the whole [earth], you may enjoy the good things produced everywhere. It is like a rich table: when [the host] has set something before each of the guests, the one reclining can take what lies beside him by merely stretching out his hand [?]. If anyone tried to go through all the other things in speech, he would run to an endless length and would not cover even a small part. For how could he, a mere human being, try to measure the infinite wisdom of God? Just consider, for now, the different kinds of plants: those that bear fruit and those that do not, those in deserts and those in inhabited lands, those on mountains and those on plains. See the variety in seeds, in herbs and in flowers, and in animals that live on land, that live both on land and in water, and that swim. Consider that everything we see exists for us: heaven, earth, sea, and everything in them. Think of someone who builds himself a splendid palace, gleaming with much gold and shining with the brilliance of precious stones. In the same way God fashioned the world and brought in the human being to rule over everything in it. And what is much more wonderful: he did not make the roof of this house of stones, but put it together from another, more precious material. Nor did he light the flame of a golden lampstand, but sent the lights from above and ordered them to run across the roof of this house, so that it would be not only useful to us but also a great delight. And he raised up the ground as a costly table. He provided all this to one who had not yet shown any good at all. Yet even when, after so great a gift, man proved ungrateful to his benefactor, God did not strip him of his honor even then. He only cast him out of paradise and punished him with that, to keep his ingratitude from going further and to check his slide toward worse. The Apostle reckoned up all these things, and more besides, since he was moved by the divine Spirit. He took in the things from the beginning and the things of every day, those done for each person and those done for all in common, the visible ones and the hidden ones, which are far more numerous than the visible, and further [150] the things of the saving plan of the only-begotten Son of God, and the good things to come. Surveying everything, in short, and gathering God's inexpressible love from every side, he reflected, as though he had fallen into a vast sea. So he learned how many and how great were the things he owed, and that he had not repaid even the smallest part. That is why he spoke these words, and examined his small sins with great precision, while consigning his good deeds to oblivion. But we are not like this. We take no account and keep no memory of our offenses, though they are many and great; yet if we do some small good, we turn it over and over, and do not stop exulting before… [Variant readings:] Savile and Morel read: "and now it is possible, just as at a rich table… each… giving… what lies beside him to take"; "and now it is possible"; "will fall in"; Morel: "will fall into." Colbert: "of those on level plains, the [?] in [?]"; [?] royal; thus. Below, Colbert: "in it, not from stones [?]… having become ungrateful toward the benefactor and having dared what he dared, not even so did he fall from his honor, but he was punished only so much as was enough for him to safeguard the good things he had been given. For, to keep his insensibility from going further and to check his slide toward worse, he imposed that punishment on him. Reckoning up all these things, the righteous man, and…" [repeated]. "…done, and further… Son of God, having reflected… he owed, the [?]. And falling into a sea"; and shortly after, "owing." "He consigned; not as we" Colbert. Below [?]: "considering these things the righteous man said"; Morel and Savile: "considering these things David also said." Below, Colbert: "his, and again of their ingratitude."

And this is clear from the following. When we hear these things from others, we grow savage, we turn into beasts, we call it an insult. So everything we do is hypocrisy. We do not even imitate the tax collector. When another man reproached him with the multitude of his sins, he accepted the reproaches and reaped the profit in deeds, for he went down justified rather than the Pharisee. But we do not even know what confession is, though we are full of countless evils. We ought not only to be convinced that we have committed countless offenses, but also to keep all our sins, small and great, written on our heart as in a book, and to mourn them as though they had just been committed. In this way we would restrain the pride of the soul, constantly reminding it of its own evils. So great a good is it to remember one's own sins that blessed Paul continually brought into the open even charges that had been wiped away. He had washed away everything earlier through baptism, and afterward lived so purely that he was conscious of nothing against himself, and he had no sins to groan over. Still, he remembered the sins before baptism that had been blotted out, saying, "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first"; and again, "He judged me faithful, appointing me to his service, though I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor and a man of violence"; "for I persecuted the church of God beyond measure and tried to destroy it"; and again, "I am not worthy to be called an apostle." For even if those sins leave us free of any liability, they are still enough to put the soul to shame and persuade it to love God intensely. Simon, for instance, was asked by the Lord which of two debtors would love the lender [152] more. He answered, "I suppose the one to whom he forgave more," and heard, "You have judged rightly." 7. When we consider the multitude of our past sins, then we will recognize how great God's grace is beyond all measure; then we will bow our heads, then we will be humbled. For the greater the offenses we are liable for, the more ashamed we will be. Paul, then, remembered even those sins. But we do not want to remember even the sins after baptism, which carry danger and make us liable to be examined for them. Even if we ever happen to think of such a thing, we immediately leap away from it, not wanting to grieve the soul with the memory even for a moment. As a result, countless evils are born to us from this useless self-indulgence. Being so insensible and soft, we cannot confess our former sins (for how could we, when we do not even train ourselves to bear their memory?), and we readily slide into further ones. Even with that memory always fresh in us and fear shaking the mind, we should be content if we can rid it of its slackness and dissipation. But if you take away this bridle as well, who will restrain it from then on, [as it runs] fearlessly down… [Variant readings:] Colbert: "the same things." Colbert: "let us restrain." Shortly after, the same: "For so great is." After [?], Colbert: "tried to destroy it, and I am not fit to be called an apostle; for even if free of liability." Colbert: "we were." Below, the same: "which also carry danger." Below, the same: "not even for a moment." [?] "of the former… we shall be able."
…I hear from those who come from there that all your time is spent in prayers and tears: [?]
